medium.resumo: The system design exercise that exposes the difference between knowing distributed systems and being trusted to operate them.
medium.conteudo_html:
The system design exercise that exposes the difference between knowing distributed systems and being trusted to operate them.

A Senior Backend Engineer candidate can spend forty minutes explaining Kafka partitions, PostgreSQL transactions, Redis caching, and Kubernetes autoscaling without giving an interviewer much evidence that they can safely own a production system. I’ve seen enough engineering discussions to know how easily technical vocabulary can substitute for actual reasoning. The architecture sounds convincing until someone introduces a failure that crosses two components.

Consider the following interview exercise. You have spent the first twenty minutes designing a payment-processing platform. Your API accepts payment requests, PostgreSQL stores transaction records, and Kafka distributes events to downstream services. The interviewer agrees that the architecture is reasonable, then changes one assumption.

A customer submits a $2,400 payment. Your service sends the request to the payment provider, but the HTTP connection times out before a response arrives. The provider may have completed the charge. Your database still says the payment is processing, and the customer presses the payment button again.

The interviewer asks you to explain exactly what your system does next.

This is where a surprising number of otherwise capable engineers begin reaching for technology names. Someone suggests retrying with exponential backoff. Another candidate introduces a distributed lock. A third proposes moving the payment operation into a Kafka consumer.

Each suggestion might have a place in a larger design. None establishes whether the original $2,400 charge occurred.

If you’re preparing for a Senior or Staff interview, understanding this distinction is worth more than memorizing another dozen architecture diagrams. It is the point where the discussion moves from implementation details to responsibility for real money.

The First Mistake: Treating a Timeout as a Failed Payment

An HTTP timeout tells you that the caller did not receive a response within its configured deadline. It does not prove that the remote operation failed.

The payment provider may have received the request, committed the charge, and attempted to send a response after the connection was already gone. Retrying the operation with a new identity could create a second charge.

A safer design begins with a durable payment operation record and a stable idempotency key. Every retry of the same logical payment must refer to that original operation, provided the payment provider supports the necessary idempotency semantics.

Payment operation: PAY-10482
Customer:         CUST-221
Amount:           2400 USD
Idempotency key:  pay-10482
Status:           UNKNOWN

Notice the status. UNKNOWN is an important outcome because it describes uncertainty without inventing a business result.

A system that converts every timeout into FAILED can encourage customers to repeat successful charges. A system that converts every timeout into SUCCESS may claim money was collected when the provider never processed the request.

The right behavior depends on what evidence the system can obtain.

The Second Mistake: Assuming Idempotency Solves Everything

An idempotency key is useful only within the contract that recognizes it.

If the payment provider guarantees that repeated requests with the same key return the result of one logical operation, retries can be much safer. But that guarantee may have a retention window, request-parameter restrictions, or specific behavior for operations that are still processing.

Your own application must also ensure that the key belongs to the correct customer and request.

CREATE TABLE payment_operations (
    operation_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id UUID NOT NULL,
    idempotency_key TEXT NOT NULL,
    amount_minor BIGINT NOT NULL,
    currency CHAR(3) NOT NULL,
    status TEXT NOT NULL,
    provider_reference TEXT,
    version BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    UNIQUE (customer_id, idempotency_key)
);

The database constraint prevents the same customer from creating multiple local payment operations with the same key. Application logic must additionally reject attempts to reuse that key with a different amount, currency, or payment intent.

This is the kind of detail that makes an interviewer pay attention. You have moved beyond saying “use idempotency” and started explaining the actual contract that preserves correctness.

For engineers preparing for payment architecture interviews: The Stripe Senior & Staff Interview Prep and Senior & Staff System Design Interview OS — Architecture Tradeoffs are relevant resources for practicing this level of reasoning.

The Third Mistake: Holding a Database Transaction Open During the Provider Call

A candidate might propose wrapping the entire payment operation in a Spring transaction.

@Transactional
public PaymentResult process(PaymentRequest request) {
    Payment payment = repository.save(createPayment(request));
    ProviderResponse response = provider.charge(request);
    payment.markCompleted(response.reference());
    return mapper.toResult(payment);
}

The code is readable. It also hides a dangerous assumption.

The database transaction cannot atomically commit or roll back the external provider’s charge. If the provider completes the payment and the local transaction later rolls back, the two systems disagree.

Keeping a database transaction open during a slow remote call also holds resources longer than necessary. Under load, that can increase connection pressure and transaction contention.

A better approach separates durable local state transitions from the external operation. The system records the payment intent, performs the provider call under a stable operation identity, and then persists the observed outcome.

There is still a crash window between the external operation and the local result update. That is why the workflow needs a recovery mechanism rather than relying on a single method call.

For Java and Spring Boot engineers: The Senior Java & Spring Boot Production Debugging OS, Spring Boot Production Troubleshooting OS, and Senior Backend Production Engineering OS are useful next steps.

The Fourth Mistake: Designing Only the Successful Path

At this point, the interviewer introduces another failure.

Your worker sends the payment request. The provider processes the charge, but the worker crashes before updating PostgreSQL. Kubernetes restarts the container, and another worker picks up the operation.

What happens now?

A reasonable design uses an explicit payment state machine.

CREATED
   |
   v
PROCESSING
   |
   +------> SUCCEEDED
   |
   +------> FAILED
   |
   +------> UNKNOWN
                |
                v
          RECONCILIATION
                |
          +-----+-----+
          |           |
          v           v
      SUCCEEDED     FAILED

This diagram is intentionally simplified. A real implementation must define valid transitions, concurrency control, and the evidence required to move from an uncertain state to a terminal state.

For example, a provider status lookup may establish that the payment succeeded. If the provider cannot determine the outcome immediately, the system may need to wait for a webhook or settlement record.

The key insight is that uncertainty is part of the domain model. Pretending it does not exist simply moves the uncertainty into production incidents and customer-support tickets.

The Fifth Mistake: Assuming a Webhook Is the Final Answer

Payment providers often send asynchronous notifications describing operation outcomes.

That helps, but webhooks may be duplicated, delayed, or delivered out of order. The application must verify their authenticity and process them according to the provider’s documented contract.

Imagine receiving a delayed payment.processing event after the payment has already reached SUCCEEDED. A naive consumer that overwrites the current state with every incoming event can regress the operation to an earlier status.

A safer consumer validates the event identity, the payment reference, and the permitted state transition. It records enough information to recognize duplicate deliveries and to investigate discrepancies.

For critical payment flows, webhook handling and reconciliation should complement each other. Neither should be treated as an excuse to ignore uncertain operations.

The Sixth Mistake: Confusing Payment Status With Financial Accounting

Suppose the provider confirms the charge. Your application updates the payment record to SUCCEEDED, and the order service begins fulfillment.

The interviewer now asks whether the customer balance is correct.

A payment status alone cannot answer that question. The financial ledger must represent the relevant postings according to the business’s accounting model.

Consider a simplified internal transfer:

Transaction: TRX-204

Customer liability account     -2400 USD
Settlement liability account   +2400 USD

Net postings:                       0 USD

The exact debit and credit directions depend on the chart of accounts and transaction type. The important principle is that the ledger preserves the accounting movements required to explain the balance.

A cached balance can be reconstructed from authoritative ledger entries. A mutable balance without transaction history cannot provide the same auditability.

This is a major difference between designing a CRUD application and designing financial infrastructure. The database can be healthy while the accounting model is wrong.

For engineers targeting fintech and high-reliability backend roles: Study the Senior Backend Engineering Architecture Decision Map, PostgreSQL Production Debugging OS, and Senior & Staff Backend Interview OS — 10 Engineering Systems.

The Seventh Mistake: Believing a Green Dashboard Means the Incident Is Over

Now imagine the payment provider experiences a twenty-minute outage.

Your API error rate returns to normal after recovery. Kubernetes shows healthy replicas, PostgreSQL connections stabilize, and Kafka consumer lag falls to zero.

The engineering team declares the incident resolved.

Unfortunately, several hundred payment operations remain in UNKNOWN, and some have been waiting for reconciliation longer than the business allows.

The infrastructure recovered, but the business workflow did not.

A production-ready system needs operational metrics that describe actual progress:

payment_operations_unknown_total
payment_operations_oldest_unknown_age_seconds
payment_reconciliation_attempts_total
payment_reconciliation_failures_total
payment_provider_discrepancies_total

The exact metric names are implementation choices. What matters is that engineers can distinguish a functioning service from a business process that has stopped making progress.

This is the kind of production detail that separates an architecture designed for a whiteboard from one designed for on-call engineers.

For production reliability preparation: The Production Incident Investigation OS, Production Incident Simulator, and On-Call Engineer Survival Guide focus on the operational side of engineering judgment.

The Eighth Mistake: Ignoring What Happens During a Deployment

The interviewer gives you one final scenario.

Your team deploys a new payment service version that introduces an additional intermediate status. Half the application instances run the new version, while the other half still run the old version during the rolling deployment.

An old worker receives an event containing the new status.

If the old code assumes that every unknown status is an error, it may repeatedly fail processing. If it maps unknown values to a default terminal state, it may corrupt the workflow.

Safe deployment requires compatibility between application versions and the data they share. Event contracts, database migrations, and state-machine changes must account for the coexistence period.

This is why deployment engineering deserves a place in system design interviews. The architecture must survive the transition between versions, not merely operate correctly after every instance has been upgraded.

For engineers responsible for production releases: The Production Deployment Checklist, Spring Boot Production Readiness OS, and Kubernetes Production Debugging OS are directly relevant.

What I Would Look for in a Strong Senior Engineer Answer

I would not expect a candidate to produce every detail of a payment platform in a forty-five-minute interview. I would expect them to recognize that an external timeout creates an uncertain outcome, that local transactions cannot guarantee atomicity across a remote provider, and that duplicate execution must be addressed at the business-operation level.

A stronger candidate would introduce a state machine, explain how reconciliation works, and identify which records are authoritative. They would also consider what happens during deployments and how the team detects workflows that remain incomplete after infrastructure recovery.

At Staff level, I would push further into organizational ownership. Who defines the payment-state contract? Which team owns reconciliation? How are accounting discrepancies investigated, and what evidence is required before a recovery job is allowed to modify financial state?

These questions reveal whether someone can make an architecture work across teams and operational boundaries.

The encouraging part is that this judgment can be learned. You do not need to have worked at a famous technology company to understand these problems. You need deliberate practice with realistic failure scenarios and the discipline to explain why your proposed solution preserves the business invariant.

How I Would Prepare for This Interview in 14 Days

I would spend the first three days implementing a small payment workflow with durable operation identities and an explicit state machine. The goal would be to make the uncertain outcome visible in the data model rather than hide it behind exceptions.

During the next four days, I would inject failures. Kill the worker after the provider call, duplicate webhook deliveries, delay responses, and restart consumers while operations are incomplete. Each experiment should produce a specific observation about the workflow’s behavior.

The following four days would focus on recovery and operations. Add reconciliation, test concurrent workers, introduce a rolling deployment, and verify that old and new application versions can coexist safely.

For the final three days, I would practice explaining the architecture aloud under interview constraints. The explanation should begin with the business invariant, establish the failure assumptions, and defend the recovery strategy without depending on a particular technology name.

A candidate who completes that exercise will have something more valuable than a memorized payment-system diagram. They will have investigated a realistic distributed workflow and developed evidence for the decisions they make.

The Next Step Depends on Where You Are Stuck

If you struggle to structure an architecture interview, begin with the Senior & Staff System Design Interview OS — 36 Architecture Diagrams or the Senior System Design Interview OS — 15 Real Scenarios. These are relevant when you need repeated practice translating requirements into designs and explaining their tradeoffs.

If your architecture answers are already strong but production failure scenarios expose gaps, the Senior Backend Production Engineering OS and Senior & Staff Backend Interview Simulator are better aligned with that problem. Engineers who want a structured combination of technical preparation and personal guidance can also explore the Senior Backend Engineering OS — 62 Systems + Mentorship.

For engineers working toward Staff or Principal roles, the Staff Engineer Architecture Decision OS, Senior to Staff & Principal Engineer OS, and Staff Engineer Behavioral Interview OS — 60 Leadership Scenarios address the broader decisions and leadership expectations that become important at those levels.

The Senior Engineer Interview & Production Playbook is another option for engineers who want to strengthen the connection between interview preparation and production engineering.

I publish additional deep technical case studies on Substack, covering Java, distributed systems, production debugging, and Senior/Staff engineering interviews.

We’re also exploring an interactive system design practice platform for engineers preparing for advanced interviews. You can request early access to the System Design Lab private beta.

medium.conteudo_html:
It’s been a long time since I wrote anything here.

Not because I ran out of things to say, but perhaps because I had too many things going on in my head and didn't know where to begin.

Life hasn't exactly been going the way I imagined it would.

My career feels uncertain. I'm trying to find internships, figure out what I actually want to do, build skills, apply for opportunities, and somehow convince myself that I will eventually land a job at one of the top MNCs I dream of working for.

And I still believe I will.

But lately, I've been thinking that getting a job isn't the only thing I want from life.

I want to build something of my own. I want to start a business someday. I want to make things easier for my family. I want financial independence, the freedom to make decisions without constantly worrying about money, and the ability to celebrate little things without feeling guilty about not doing enough.

I want to explore different things, learn, fail, try again, and experience life outside the four walls of a career plan.

Yet, somehow, I feel stuck between wanting to do everything and not knowing where to start.

I have so many dreams, but lately, I haven't been able to organize my own thoughts, let alone my life.

And then there's the part of life we don't always know how to talk about.

Relationships.

It was my first time being emotionally involved with someone in that way. I think I was learning things about myself that I had never really noticed before. How I react. How attached I can become. How little things can affect my mood. How sometimes, when emotions get overwhelming, I don't know how to respond calmly.

Recently, I've found myself getting irritated more easily. Reacting to things I would probably have handled differently before. Feeling emotions intensely and then wondering why I reacted that way in the first place.

It's strange when you realize that you're not quite feeling like yourself.

I don't want to blame anyone for everything I'm feeling. I also don't want to pretend that everything is fine when it isn't.

Maybe I'm simply learning that emotions need to be understood, not just acted upon.

And honestly, I don't have all the answers yet.

---

I want my life to feel like mine again.

I want to wake up with things I'm excited about.

I want to work on projects, learn something interesting, explore business ideas, get an internship, build a career, spend time with my family, laugh over stupid things, and celebrate small wins without waiting for some huge achievement to give me permission.

I want to stop feeling like I'm falling behind every time I look at someone else's progress.

I know I cannot become everything I want to be in a single year, a month, or even a few weeks. Maybe that's something I need to remind myself more often.

A career takes time.

Building a business takes time.

Understanding yourself takes time.

And perhaps becoming emotionally mature takes even more time than we expect.

---

I'm not writing this because I suddenly figured life out.

I'm writing because I haven't.

Maybe this is my way of starting again, without a perfect plan, without pretending to be the most productive person in the room, and without having to turn every difficult experience into a lesson immediately.

I still have big dreams.

I still want to work at great companies, build something meaningful, become financially independent, and create a life where my family has more opportunities and fewer worries.

But I also want to enjoy the process.

I want to notice the small happiness happening while I'm busy waiting for the big ones.

So, maybe this is where I begin again.

Not with a five-year plan.

Not with a promise that I'll never lose focus again.

Just with the intention of showing up, trying things, learning to manage my emotions, and making a little more sense of my life, one day at a time.

I don't know exactly where life is taking me. But I hope I don't forget to live while I'm figuring it out.

And maybe, for now, that's enough.

Utils ini digunakan untuk pengecekan apakah sudah login dan role user tsb adalah admin. Utils ini digunakan ketika sebelum melakukan CRUD dan untuk membatasi route api kita.

import type { H3Event } from "h3";
import {
  serverSupabaseUser,
  serverSupabaseServiceRole,

} from "#supabase/server";

export async function requireAdmin(event: H3Event) {
  const claims = await serverSupabaseUser(event);

  const adminId = claims?.sub;
  if (!adminId) {
    throw createError({ statusCode: 401, statusMessage: "Unauthorized" });
  }

  const admin = serverSupabaseServiceRole<any>(event);
  const { data, error } = await admin
    .from("users")
    .select("role")
    .eq("id", adminId)
    .single();

  if (error || data?.role !== "admin") {
    throw createError({ statusCode: 404, statusMessage: "Not Found" });
  }

  return { adminId, admin };
}

  // useState: di-cache & ikut terkirim dari server ke client (tanpa fetch ulang)
  const profile = useState<Profile | null>("profile", () => null);

  const fetchProfile = async (force = false): Promise<Profile | null> => {
    const id = user.value?.sub;
    if (!id) {
      profile.value = null;
      return null;
    }
    if (!force && profile.value?.id === id) return profile.value;

    // RLS: user hanya bisa select baris miliknya sendiri (admin: semua)
    const { data, error } = await supabase
      .from("users")
      .select("id, name, email, role")
      .eq("id", id)
      .single();

    if (error) {
      console.error("fetchProfile:", error.message);
      profile.value = null;
      return null;
    }
    profile.value = data as Profile;
    return profile.value;
  };

  const isAdmin = computed(() => profile.value?.role === "admin");

  return { profile, isAdmin, fetchProfile };
};

corrida_no_ar.resumo: Médicos e corredoras alertam para os riscos do uso de testosterona na menopausa. Hyrox intensifica controle antidoping. Vencedor da Maratona de NY foca na pista. Provas em Buenos Aires e no Rio com novidades. E a dúvida: qual a vantagem de correr de macaquinho?
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Quarta-feira | 18 de novembro de 2026

O uso de testosterona na reposição hormonal durante a menopausa tem sido um tema polêmico, especialmente no esporte. Enquanto algumas mulheres aceitam o tratamento, outras recusam por saber que a substância é considerada doping. A corredora Clarissa compartilhou sua experiência: mesmo sem estar na menopausa, um profissional da área médica e do esporte sugeriu que ela fizesse reposição com testosterona para melhorar a disposição e a performance. Ela prontamente recusou, afirmando: “Mas isso é doping, não pode”. Clarissa destaca que muitas mulheres, buscando alívio para os sintomas da menopausa ou melhora no desempenho, acabam aceitando o tratamento sem saber que a substância é proibida no esporte.

O alerta é reforçado pela Dra. Andréa Benazzi, ginecologista, que se diz muito preocupada com a prescrição indiscriminada de hormônios anabolizantes, como a testosterona, através de implantes. Ela relata um aumento de doenças cardiovasculares, hepáticas, endocrinológicas e psiquiátricas em mulheres que utilizam esses tratamentos. Segundo a médica, a prescrição de testosterona na menopausa só é recomendada em casos específicos de transtorno do desejo sexual hipoativo, com diagnóstico confirmado. No Congresso Mundial de Menopausa, ela notou uma grande preocupação de cardiologistas, que buscam alertar sobre os riscos. A “Carta do Rio”, um documento assinado por 13 sociedades médicas brasileiras e pela International Menopause Society, foi criada como uma tentativa de frear a comercialização e o uso desses implantes hormonais sem a devida comprovação científica e segurança.

Hyrox implementa antidoping fora de competição

A franquia de competições Hyrox deu um passo importante para se alinhar com as exigências de um esporte olímpico, seu objetivo futuro. A organização oficializou a implementação de testes antidoping fora do período de competição e sem aviso prévio. A medida, que já era aplicada durante os eventos, agora será estendida, aumentando o rigor contra o uso de substâncias proibidas.

Fla Run está de volta ao Rio

A Fla Run 2026, corrida oficial do Flamengo, acontecerá no dia 29 de novembro no Aterro do Flamengo, no Rio de Janeiro. O evento contará com percursos de 3, 5 e 10 km. Se você é torcedor rubro-negro e quer participar, pode usar o cupom CORRIDANOAR10 para garantir um desconto na sua inscrição.

Vencedor de NY foca na pista

Após uma estreia espetacular e a vitória na Maratona de Nova York, o sueco Andreas Almgren anunciou que voltará seu foco para as pistas de atletismo. Ele não está satisfeito com seu tempo de 26:52 nos 10.000 metros e acredita que pode baixar essa marca em pelo menos 30 segundos. A tentativa acontecerá no dia 6 de junho, em Estocolmo. A estratégia de alternar entre maratonas e provas de pista para ganhar velocidade é a mesma que era utilizada pelo brasileiro Marilson Gomes dos Santos, que também já venceu a Maratona de Nova York.

Buenos Aires exige comprovação de tempo na largada

Para melhorar a experiência na largada, a Meia e a Maratona de Buenos Aires atualizaram seus critérios. Agora, para largar nos pelotões C e D, será obrigatório comprovar tempo. Para a meia maratona, o curral C exigirá tempo abaixo de 1h15, e o D, entre 1h16 e 1h30. Quem não tiver tempo de 21k, poderá usar uma marca de 10k: sub-35min para o curral C e sub-41min para o D. Na maratona, o curral C será para tempos abaixo de 3h, e o D, para marcas entre 3h01 e 3h30. A comprovação também poderá ser feita com um tempo de meia maratona: sub-1h25 para o curral C e sub-1h39 para o D.

Últimas vagas para a Uphill Corcovado

Ainda dá tempo de se inscrever para a Uphill Corcovado, que acontece neste fim de semana no Rio de Janeiro. A prova, que leva os corredores a um dos pontos turísticos mais famosos do mundo, tem distâncias de 5, 10 e 21 km.
